credit_line: Project ORCON film, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (c. 1948-53), via Internet Archive
what_it_shows: 179 s, 852x480, 29.97 fps, colour then B&W, silent. 0:00 title card 'PROJECT ORCON / ORganic CONtrol'. 0:03-0:22 hands fit an attachment to a pigeon's beak (consistent with Skinner's 'gold electrode' on the beak tip, which is not captioned). 0:24-0:38 pigeon in a harness or jacket. 0:40-1:02 pigeon pecks at a small aperture in a panel. 1:08-1:34 a striped (semiconducting?) plate, with a pencil pointing to its centre. 1:36-2:05 pigeon seen from behind, pecking at the plate. 2:10-2:46 the hero shot: a backlit circular screen showing a ship at sea with the pigeon in silhouette pecking at it. 2:48 the ship image tilts. 2:52-2:59 end title 'ORCON' with a pigeon flapping. This is post-war Navy ORCON footage, NOT the 1943 Pelican nose cone.
best_segments: 2:10-2:46 silhouette pecking at the ship on the round screen: use in S2 (mechanism), with a 9:16 centre crop on the circle. 0:24-0:38 harnessed pigeon for S3. 0:00-0:02 title card for S4 or the end. 1:08-1:20 plate with pointer for the diagram transition. Speed ramps are fine; there is no audio to keep.

license: Public domain: US federal government work by the National Bureau of Standards (now NIST), Commons tag {{PD-USGov-NIST}}
credit_line: 'Pelican' guided glide bomb (SWOD Mk 7), National Bureau of Standards / NIST, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: The real Pelican (SWOD Mk 7) glider, the air-to-ground missile Skinner's pigeons were meant to steer. Side view, hung from a crane hook against a white backdrop, with twin tail booms and round end plates (numbered '64') and a bulbous dark nose. Field-test instrumentation is shown (per the Commons description: camera mounts under the wing and a lamp panel housed in the nose). 5558x4343 px. NOTE: this is the radar-homing test version, not a pigeon nose.
best_segments: S1 hook ('steer missiles'): slow push toward the nose. S2 open. Crop the nose for 9:16.

license: Public domain: US federal government work by the National Bureau of Standards (now NIST), Commons tag {{PD-USGov-NIST}}
credit_line: Pelican radar receiving equipment, National Bureau of Standards / NIST, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: The Pelican's electronic (radar receiving) guidance kit laid out on white: black boxes, cables and a dish antenna. Per Commons, 'it carried only receiving radio equipment, the transmitter carried instead on the mother plane'. 5257x3667 px.
best_segments: S4 result, as the electronics that replaced the birds. Optional.

license: Public domain: US federal government work by the National Bureau of Standards (now NIST), Commons tag {{PD-USGov-NIST}}
credit_line: SWOD Mark 7 'Pelican', National Bureau of Standards / NIST, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_it_shows: An alternative scan of the same Pelican on a hoist. It is higher contrast, and the nose number '6' is readable. 5377x4313 px.
best_segments: Alternative to 02. The nose '6' reads well in a tight crop.
